meta.title: MCP Question Bank — Chapter 11: JSON-RPC 2.0 Fundamentals
meta.revision: v2.1 (curated 2026-09-12, 200 items, verified against the 2026-07-28 specification)

questions.question: Your server receives a JSON-RPC notification it cannot process. What is the correct behaviour?

options.text: Send no JSON-RPC response at all; on HTTP the POST itself may be answered with an error status
Return a JSON-RPC error response that echoes the notification's method name in place of the missing id
Queue the notification and answer it once the client sends its next request
Return a JSON-RPC error response with id null so the client can correlate it

questions.explanation: The receiver MUST NOT send a JSON-RPC response to a notification. Over Streamable HTTP an accepted notification gets 202 with no body; one the server cannot accept gets an HTTP error status, whose body MAY carry a JSON-RPC error with no id.

questions.question: A client sends {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":null,"method":"tools/list"}. How must an MCP server treat it?

options.text: As a notification, since a null id signals that no response is expected
As a valid request, assigning it the next unused integer id when the response is built
As a valid request, answering with a response whose id is also null
As an invalid request: MCP forbids null ids, which base JSON-RPC merely discourages

questions.explanation: MCP tightens JSON-RPC here: request ids MUST be a string or integer and MUST NOT be null. A notification is a message with no id member at all, which is different from an id whose value is null.

questions.question: Which standard JSON-RPC code does an MCP server use when the JSON body cannot be parsed at all?

options.text: -32700 Parse error
-32602 Invalid params
-32603 Internal error
-32600 Invalid Request

questions.explanation: -32700 is for invalid JSON. -32600 is for JSON that parses but is not a valid request object, such as a wrong jsonrpc value or a null id in MCP. -32602 covers bad params, including a missing required _meta field.

questions.question: While debugging you find a response object that carries both a result member and an error member. What is wrong with it?

options.text: Nothing: result carries the payload and error carries any warnings raised
A response may carry both, but the client must then ignore the result
A response may carry both, but only when the id member is null
A response must contain exactly one of result or error, never both

questions.explanation: JSON-RPC 2.0 makes result and error mutually exclusive: exactly one must be present. There is no warnings channel on a success response, and the id member has no bearing on which one appears.

questions.question: A client built for 2026-07-28 receives a result object with no resultType field. What must it do?

options.text: Re-issue the request with a new id, because the result was truncated
Reject it as invalid, since resultType is required on every result
Treat it as "complete", as earlier-protocol servers had no resultType
Treat it as "input_required" and wait for the inputRequests to arrive

questions.explanation: resultType is required in this revision, but for backwards compatibility clients MUST treat an absent resultType as "complete". By contrast, a resultType value the client does not recognise MUST be considered invalid.

questions.question: A client POSTs a JSON array containing two requests to an MCP endpoint. What should happen?

options.text: The server answers with an array of two responses, in any order, matched by id
The server rejects it: an MCP POST body must be a single request or notification
The server answers with an array of two responses, in the order received
The server processes the first request and ignores the rest of the array

questions.explanation: Base JSON-RPC allows batches, but MCP does not use them: each Streamable HTTP POST body is exactly one request or notification, and each stdio line is one message.
